text: The cloud isn't one single deployment model — there's public cloud, private cloud, and hybrid cloud, and the real difference between all three boils down to one question: who owns the underlying hardware, and is it being shared with other customers or not?

Public cloud, like AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud, is multi-tenant: the exact same physical hardware and datacenters serve many different customers at once, kept isolated from each other by the hypervisor. Private cloud is infrastructure dedicated to a single organization only, whether it physically sits on-premises in that company's own datacenter, or is hosted by an outside vendor on hardware set aside exclusively for them. Hybrid cloud connects both of those worlds together over a private, dedicated link — something like Azure ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN — so workloads on either side can talk to each other securely, without ever routing over the open internet.

Here's what that looks like in a realistic scenario: a bank keeps its core transaction database on-premises, inside its own datacenter, because of strict data-residency requirements that won't allow that data to leave. But it still runs its customer-facing web application in Azure, connected back to that on-prem database through ExpressRoute. Customers get a modern, scalable web experience, and the regulated data never actually has to leave the bank's own walls.

Companies choose hybrid cloud for real, specific reasons, not out of indecision: compliance and data-residency rules that force certain data to stay within a particular location or jurisdiction, latency when a workload needs to sit physically close to on-premises equipment like factory-floor sensors, legacy systems too old or too fragile to re-architect for the cloud any time soon, and gradual migration — moving to the cloud piece by piece instead of all at once, to spread risk out and let a team learn as it goes.

Most new companies, with no existing datacenter investment and no unusual regulatory burden, simply start out in the public cloud, since it's the path of least operational overhead. Next lesson: regions and availability zones — how cloud providers structure their own datacenters so that one single facility going down doesn't take your entire application down with it.
